quickSummary: In 1875, Sachs classified plant tissues into Epidermal, Ground, and Vascular systems. The Epidermis features a protective waxy Cuticle (absent in roots) and Stomatal Apparatuses: Dicots possess kidney/bean-shaped guard cells (thick inelastic inner wall, thin elastic outer wall); Monocot grasses possess dumb-bell-shaped guard cells (bulbous thin ends, thick middle shaft).

conceptBreakdown.content: In 1875, Julius von Sachs categorized plant tissues into three fundamental tissue systems based on their structural positioning and physiological specialization across plant organs.

conceptBreakdown.content:
Forms the outermost protective covering of the primary plant body.

### Structural Components
• **Epidermis & Cuticle**: Single continuous layer of parenchymatous cells coated externally by a waxy hydrophobic layer of cutin (**Cuticle**), which restricts cuticular transpiration (*Cuticle is strictly ABSENT in roots*).
• **Stomatal Apparatus**: Comprises three interrelated structures: **Stomatal Pore + Guard Cells + Subsidiary (Accessory) Cells**.
• **Guard Cell Morphologies**:
  - **Dicots**: Kidney- or bean-shaped; inner wall facing the pore is thick and inelastic, outer wall is thin and highly elastic.
  - **Monocot Grasses**: Dumb-bell-shaped; bulbous ends are thin-walled and expandable, while the middle constricted shaft is heavily thickened.
• **Epidermal Appendages**:
  - **Root Hairs**: Unicellular, unbranched tubular extensions of root epidermal (epiblema/rhizodermis) cells that absorb capillary water.
  - **Trichomes**: Multicellular, branched or unbranched epidermal hairs on stems that prevent excessive transpiration and secrete chemical defenses.
